remarks: This record is FGD-only (Mode B) and has not been verified against an official ED source — WB.json has no ED entry for CTE.

A Fire NOC-style renewal/garbage-tax linkage was raised by participants in this CTE session ('renewal is not given unless the garbage tax is paid'); it is reported here as stated, though it may pertain to a related renewal process rather than the initial Consent to Establish itself — the transcript does not fully disambiguate this.
Overall, apart from the issues raised, participants said they were broadly fine with the process, the documents required and the fees.

findings.text: The Shilpasathi portal, which carries all three services, stays down or glitches often — reported outages of 20 days to over a month at a time with no prior notice; even when working, network/connectivity issues slow the process.
Rejections are not shown with a reason; applicants have to visit the department and meet different officers to learn what is wrong, adding time and cost.

About 90% of participants use consultants or intermediaries — not because documents are hard to understand but because they cannot spend the time chasing papers and offices; the consultant's fee is on top of the government fee.
Renewal needs the garbage tax to be paid to the local corporation first; hospital participants said they pay a waste tax as well as a hefty fee to the bio-waste disposal agency for the same waste.
A participant said even a small hospital expansion (e.g. adding five dialysis beds to a 50-bed unit) seems to need a fresh consent.
Participants said it is hard to complete the process without a consultant because of limited awareness among applicants.

There is no deemed approval, but a deemed-rejection rule exists: an application not moved within one month is automatically rejected, which during a long portal outage can reject applications through no fault of the applicant.
Several overlapping charges on the same waste disposal (waste tax plus bio-waste disposal agency fee) were named as putting an undue financial burden on organisations.
Linking licence renewal to payment of the garbage tax to the corporation was named as one of the major problems.

Consent timelines and validity were stated for context: approval time is 15 days for Green category and 30 days for Red and Orange; validity is 15 years for Green, 10 years for Orange and 5 years for Red.

Process as described: the applicant fills the form and uploads documents on the portal; auto-scrutiny gives either a recommendation or a list of reasons to work on; if all is in order the fee is shown and paid online (challan generated), then approval follows.
A tracking system exists, but participants said they got no usable tracking, only rejections without reasons; status messages by email, SMS or the portal were not clear enough.

Although everything is submitted online, applicants still go to departments to understand rejections; participants wanted department queries to be raised online too, instead of requiring office visits.
The portal has workflow problems in addition to the downtime, per the session recap.
No redundant document was identified; participants said the documents asked for are reasonable and none should be removed or reduced, and the fee structure is also stated on the portal.
Give advance notice of portal downtime (a couple of days' notice was mentioned) so applicants can time their applications.
Show reasons for rejection on the portal and let applicants resolve queries online, so office visits are not needed.
Improve tracking and alerts with clear status updates by email or SMS on each stage.
Review and rationalise overlapping waste taxes and charges, especially for hospitals.
Hold more awareness sessions, and hold future FGDs by zone (e.g. South and North Kolkata) so that more people can attend.

steps.title: Final building plan sanction
steps.note: Issued once all departmental requirements/recommendations are satisfied; timing was highly variable in participant accounts.

remarks: This record is FGD-only (Mode B) and has not been verified against an official ED source — WB.json has no ED entry for FBPA.

One participant's application took about three years (2022 to sanction on 10 August 2025); the delay was linked to the early stage of UODB implementation and created difficulty meeting a lease condition requiring production to start within three years in a government industrial estate.
The discussion also touched on related regulatory matters (factory/fire/forest licensing) but these were not treated as primary findings for Factory Building Plan Approval.

findings.text: Approval timelines vary significantly across municipalities/locations; some applications were approved within about 15 days, while others took 2.5 months to 3 years.

Applications submitted through the single-window/UODB system require coordination among departments such as fire, drainage, water and building authorities, and this coordination was not always streamlined.

One participant's application submitted around 2022 took about three years to receive sanction (granted 10 August 2025), linked to the early stage of the UODB system and inter-departmental coordination issues.

Without the building plan sanction the participant could not construct/operationalise the factory, and the delay created difficulty meeting a requirement to start production within three years of a lease in a government industrial estate.
Even where applications are submitted online, processing times differ substantially — some cases 15-20 days, others more than a year or 2-3 years.
Some participants used consultants/LBS because the process was considered time-consuming or because they were unfamiliar with the procedure.

Separate requirements/recommendations from departments such as fire, water and drainage were described before sanction, including instances where modifications such as an additional staircase were required.
Participants raised concerns about limited status updates or communication during application processing.
There is no clearly defined time-bound approval framework ensuring a consistent timeline for departments to process and grant Factory Building Plan Approval.
There is no clear deemed-approval mechanism or other automatic resolution when a department does not respond within the prescribed timeline.
Although applications are submitted through the single-window system, coordination among concerned departments is not fully streamlined, requiring applicants to follow up with multiple departments.
There is no clearly defined single point of contact or dedicated support mechanism for resolving application-related issues and providing procedural guidance.
Clear and comprehensive guidance on the online application process and departmental requirements appears limited, particularly for applicants using the relatively new online system.
Applications require coordination among multiple departments (fire, water, drainage and other authorities) before final building plan sanction.

No specific duplicate-document requirement was clearly established for FBPA; participants referred to multiple departmental requirements/clearances on the same building plan, but the transcript does not provide enough evidence to classify these as duplicate documents.
Ensure a clearly defined and consistently followed timeline for Factory Building Plan Approval.
Strengthen coordination among all departments involved in the approval process through the single-window/UODB system.
Introduce a single point of contact or dedicated helpline for application-related queries and coordination, and provide regular status updates to applicants.
Consider a deemed-approval/automatic-processing mechanism where an application remains pending beyond the prescribed statutory timeline, subject to the applicable legal framework.
Participants generally acknowledged that online application is useful, but said its effectiveness depends on coordination among the departments involved.

remarks: This record is FGD-only (Mode B) and has not been verified against an official ED source — WB.json has no ED entry for RFNO.

Participants balanced their complaints against an acknowledgement of the importance of fire-safety standards, asking specifically for a more predictable, transparent and consistent renewal process rather than for safety requirements to be relaxed.

findings.text: Renewal timelines are prolonged and unpredictable: some completed within 2-3 months, but many large projects faced delays of several months to over a year; one application remained pending for four months even after inspection and submission.

Different inspectors prescribe different compliance measures during successive renewals even when there are no changes in the building or applicable guidelines; in some cases an application accepted by one official was later questioned by a higher authority for the same deficiency.
When inspectors or approving officers were transferred, the incoming officer often reassessed the file and sought additional documents or fresh inspections, interrupting continuity of processing.

Documents already available with the department or online portal had to be submitted again for subsequent renewals; older buildings (20-30 years old) were asked for sanctioned plans and historical records that either did not exist or no longer reflected the current structure.

Participants reported waiting several months to receive inspection recommendations, and found it difficult to determine the exact stage of their application or the reasons for delay, leading to repeated follow-ups with departmental officials.
Participants felt some newly appointed officers lacked sufficient technical expertise, contributing to differing interpretations, repeated inspections and conflicting recommendations.

Delays could prevent businesses from commencing or continuing operations and affect rental income, operational revenue and project viability; participants reported additional consultancy/compliance costs, with some estimating losses of ₹60-70 lakh per month in specific cases.

Businesses reported having to undertake costly structural changes, such as rebuilding staircases or fire exits, during renewal even though the same infrastructure had been covered by an earlier Fire NOC.

The reported variation in compliance requirements across officers and renewal cycles indicates an absence of sufficiently uniform guidelines for renewal inspections; participants sought a standardized basis for assessment.
There is no policy for legacy buildings and historical documentation — older establishments may lack sanctioned plans, or available records may no longer correspond to the present structure.

There is no continuity framework for previously approved fire-safety infrastructure; it can still be subjected to fresh modification requirements during renewal even when premises/conditions have not materially changed.
There is no continuity mechanism when officers are transferred — applications may be reassessed from scratch rather than continuing from the stage already reached.
There is no document-reuse policy — documents already held by the department may still be requested again during each renewal.
Participants reported limited accountability for delays beyond prescribed timelines, with applications able to remain pending for months without clear consequence.
The portal does not allow applicants to update registered mobile numbers or email IDs, which can disrupt communication when the responsible personnel change.

Limited transparency and reliance on manual follow-up: applicants found it difficult to track the exact stage of the application and often had to contact officials personally or make repeated visits for updates.
Standardize inspection practices and technical interpretation across officers, with regular training on fire-safety norms.
Ensure continuity when officers are transferred, so applications continue from their existing stage rather than restarting unnecessarily.
Introduce document reuse and a single source of records, with appropriate treatment of historical records for legacy buildings, so applicants provide only documents that changed.
Enable updating of registered contact details on the portal so communication is not interrupted when responsible personnel change.

Suggested standardized inspection guidelines with officer training, continuity of processing across officer transfers, a document-reuse policy, and the ability to update registered contact details on the portal.
